title: Manipulation and Grasping

mentor.name: PALM-3
mentor.character: Puts the object in your hand before the maths, and asks which way it would slide if you let go a little.

summary: You will decide where a hand should touch an object, prove the grip can resist the forces the world pushes back with, and close the fingers with the force the part survives. By the end you can score candidate grasps, run a guarded approach, control contact force instead of position, and react to slip before the part is on the floor.

lessons.title: The Part on the Bench
lessons.goal: Compute the gravity force vector on a part and decide whether it is inside the gripper payload rating.
lessons.theory:
Everything in this workshop starts with a part sitting on a bench and a hand that has to pick it up. The arm already knows how to reach the pose, that was the Joint Cathedral. What nobody has told it yet is whether the part will still be in the fingers a second later.

The first number is the easy one. A part of mass `m` pulls down with `m` times `g`, and in the workshop frame `z` points up, so the weight of a part is `np.array([0.0, 0.0, -mass * G])` newtons with `G` at 9.81. A 420 g aluminium bracket pulls with 4.12 N, which sounds like nothing until you remember it has to go through two rubber pads and a friction coefficient.

The second number comes off the datasheet. A Robotiq 2F-85 is rated for 5 kg with the right friction and a fraction of that with a smooth cup. That rating is not the arm payload and it is not a suggestion: past it the fingers back drive and the part walks out of the jaws under acceleration.

So the very first thing a pick routine does is refuse. Weight in, verdict out, before a single joint moves.

lessons.title: Where the Finger Touches
lessons.goal: Compute the inward unit normal of a contact point on a box shaped part.
lessons.theory:
A contact is not a point. It is a point plus a direction, and the direction is the one thing beginners drop.

The **inward normal** at a contact is the unit vector that points from the surface into the material. It matters because a finger can only ever **push**, never pull: the force it applies has to have a positive component along that inward normal. Get the sign backwards in your code and the maths will happily tell you a grip is stable while the fingers are sucking on the part.

For an axis aligned box of half sizes `half` the normal is found by asking which face the point sits on. Scale each coordinate by its own half size into `ratios`, and the largest one names the face. Then `axis = int(np.argmax(ratios))` picks it and `n[axis] = -np.sign(point[axis])` turns it inward, because a contact at positive x on the right face pushes towards negative x.

The pads of a 2F-85 are 20 mm squares, so a real contact is a patch and this point is its centre. That approximation carries the whole first half of this course.
lessons.task: Fill in `inward_normal(point, half)` so it returns the unit inward normal at that surface point, and check each contact with the `points_inward` test already written.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

HALF = np.array([0.030, 0.020, 0.045])
CONTACTS = [
    np.array([0.030, 0.000, 0.010]),
    np.array([-0.030, 0.005, -0.020]),
    np.array([0.000, 0.000, 0.045]),
]


def inward_normal(point, half):
    ratios = np.abs(point) / half
    axis = int(np.argmax(ratios))
    n = np.zeros(3)
    n[axis] = -np.sign(point[axis])
    return n


def points_inward(point, n):
    return bool(np.dot(n, -point) > 0.0)


for p in CONTACTS:
    n = inward_normal(p, HALF)
    print("at", np.round(p, 3), "normal", np.round(n, 3),
          "unit", bool(abs(np.linalg.norm(n) - 1.0) < 1e-9),
          "inward", points_inward(p, n))
lessons.hint: Start with `ratios = np.abs(point) / half`, then write the two lines the teoria spells out.

lessons.title: Straight In and Sideways
lessons.goal: Split a contact force into its normal component and its tangential component in the contact plane.
lessons.theory:
Every contact force splits into two parts that behave nothing alike.

The part along the normal is the squeeze. It is bounded below by zero, because a finger cannot pull, and bounded above by what the part survives. The part in the tangent plane is friction, and it is bounded by the squeeze itself. That asymmetry is the whole reason grasping is hard: you buy tangential capacity by spending normal force on a part that may not want it.

The split is a projection you already know. The normal component of a force `f` against unit normal `n` is `np.dot(f, n) * n`, and whatever is left, `f - normal_part(f, n)`, lies in the plane of the pad. The scalar `np.dot(f, n)` on its own is the number a load cell behind the fingertip would report.

In the demonstration one contact is a clean push straight down the normal and the other arrives at an angle. The second one is the interesting case, because most of its magnitude is doing nothing for the grip.
lessons.task: Fill in `normal_part(f, n)` and `tangent_part(f, n)` so the two components add back to the original force, and read which of the two contacts is wasting its magnitude.
lessons.hint: Both expressions are written out in the teoria, and the second one is defined in terms of the first.

lessons.title: The Twist a Push Makes
lessons.goal: Turn a contact force into a six dimensional wrench about the object centre of mass.
lessons.theory:
A force applied off centre does two things at once: it pushes and it turns. Adding the turn is what promotes a force to a **wrench**, the six number object that the rest of this course speaks in.

Stack the three force components first and the three moment components second. The moment of a force `f` applied at a lever arm `r` measured from the centre of mass is the cross product, so the whole wrench is `np.concatenate([f, np.cross(r, f)])`. Ordering matters and there is no convention police: pick force first, moment second, and never mix it with a library that does the opposite.

The useful scalar that falls out is the perpendicular distance from the centre of mass to the line of the force, which is `np.linalg.norm(np.cross(r, f)) / np.linalg.norm(f)`. Push straight at the centre of mass and that distance is zero, no matter how far away your finger is. That is why a pick on the geometric middle of a badly balanced casting still spins it: the lever arm is measured to the mass, not to the shape.
lessons.task: Fill in `wrench(r, f)` and `lever(r, f)`, then compare a contact aimed at the centre of mass against one that misses it by 40 mm.
lessons.hint: Both formulas are written in the teoria. Wrap the second one in `float(` so the print stays a plain number.

lessons.title: What the Hand Leaves Over
lessons.goal: Sum every contact wrench plus gravity and read the residual wrench the object is left holding.
lessons.theory:
A grasp holds when the contacts cancel everything the world does to the object. Sum the wrenches, subtract gravity, and whatever survives is the **residual**: the wrench that is going to accelerate the part out of the hand.

The accumulation is a loop, `net = net + wrench(r, f)`, and gravity enters on the vertical force row with `net[2] = net[2] - mass * G`. Nothing else is subtle here, which is precisely why it is worth writing once: from now on every quality metric, every slip test and every disturbance budget in this course is a question about this residual.

The demonstration runs two grips on the same 600 g block. The first is two fingers pressing straight in, equal and opposite, perfectly balanced sideways and holding nothing up. The second adds the friction forces the pads actually generate. Read the vertical row of both and you will see the exact reason a grip with no friction term is a grip that drops.

lessons.title: Held Without Being Squeezed
lessons.goal: Decide whether a contact blocks a candidate object motion from the sign of the normal component.
lessons.theory:
There are two ways to hold something. **Form closure** holds it with geometry alone: the fingers are placed so that no motion of the object is possible, and you could switch the motors off. **Force closure** holds it with friction: the object could move, but the contacts can generate whatever wrench is needed to stop it. A drill chuck is form closure. Two rubber pads on a glass jar are force closure.

Form closure is the cleaner idea, so it goes first. Its whole machinery is one test: does this contact block that motion?

A finger can push into the object and nothing else. So a contact with inward normal `n` forbids exactly the motions whose velocity at the contact point has a negative component along `n`, since those would drive the surface into the finger. Positive means the object is leaving the finger and the contact simply opens. Zero means sliding along the pad, which geometry alone allows. That is `float(np.dot(n, v)) < 0.0`, and it is the only inequality in this chapter.

The demonstration squeezes a bar between two flat pads and asks about four directions. Two of them nobody stops.

lessons.title: The Motion Nobody Stops
lessons.goal: Compute the velocity of a material point under a planar twist and use it to test whether a candidate twist survives every contact.
lessons.theory:
Objects do not only translate. A planar rigid motion is a **twist**, three numbers, two of linear velocity and one of angular velocity, and every material point of the body moves at a different speed under it.

The velocity of the point at position `r`, measured from the centre of the object, is the translation plus the rotation carried around by the lever arm. In the plane the cross product collapses to a quarter turn, so it is `twist[0:2] + twist[2] * np.array([-r[1], r[0]])`. Now the blocking test of the last lesson can be asked at each contact with the right velocity instead of the body velocity.

A twist **survives** a set of contacts when no contact blocks it, so `blocks(n, point_velocity(t, r))` is false everywhere. A surviving twist is a way the object can still move, which means it is a way the object can still leave.

Watch the pure rotation in the demonstration. Two flat pads on the sides of a bar do not block it at all, because at both contacts the surface slides along the pad instead of into it. That is the escape route that every two finger pinch has and no amount of squeezing removes.

lessons.hint: The velocity formula is in the teoria. In `survives`, loop the contacts and `return False` the moment `blocks(n, point_velocity(t, r))` is true.

lessons.title: Four Pads, Two Verdicts
lessons.goal: Sample the twist space and give a form closure verdict, then show two four contact layouts that disagree.
lessons.theory:
Form closure means **no** twist survives. That is a statement about an infinite set, and the honest engineering answer is to sample it densely and see whether anything gets through.

One detail decides whether the sampling means anything: units. A twist mixes metres per second with radians per second, and if you sample a unit sphere in those raw numbers, a 30 mm part turns rotation into a rounding error and every rotational escape hides. So the sampler scales the angular row by the part radius, `t[2] / RADIUS`, which makes a radian per second comparable with the surface speed it produces. That helper is written for you.

With the sampler in place the verdict is short. Collect `survivors = [t for t in twists if survives(contacts, t)]` and the grip is form closure when `len(survivors) == 0`.

The demonstration runs two four contact layouts on the same bar. One puts the pads on the middle of each face, which is what everybody draws. The other slides each pad off centre. The count of fingers is identical and only one of them holds.

lessons.title: Rank Says Maybe
lessons.goal: Build the contact wrench matrix, read its rank, and show that full rank does not imply form closure.
lessons.theory:
There is a cheap test that people reach for instead of sampling, and it is worth knowing exactly how much it buys.

Each frictionless contact can only push along its normal, and that push produces one wrench on the object. In the plane the wrench of contact `(r, n)` is the row `np.array([n[0], n[1], r[0] * n[1] - r[1] * n[0]])`, two force components and the moment about the object centre. Stack those rows and you have the contact wrench matrix. Its rank counts how many independent directions the fingers can push in at all, out of the three a planar body has.

Rank below three is a proof of failure: some direction has nobody pushing along it. Rank three is **not** a proof of success, because the fingers might all push on the same side of that direction and never be able to pull back. Rank ignores signs, and signs are the entire problem.

The demonstration shows the gap directly. Two layouts, both with `np.linalg.matrix_rank` equal to three, and the sampler from the last lesson finds an escape in one of them.

lessons.title: How Wide Is It, Really
lessons.goal: Compute the width of a polygonal part along a direction and find the direction where it is narrowest.
lessons.theory:
A jaw does not care about the bounding box of a part. It cares about the width the part shows **along the line the jaws close on**, and that number changes with every degree of rotation.

The width along a unit direction `d` is the span of the projections of the vertices, so `proj = poly @ d` and the answer is `float(proj.max() - proj.min())`. That is the support function of the shape, and for a convex polygon the vertices are enough: no interior point can stick out past them.

Two of those widths have names worth keeping. The **minimum width** over all directions is the narrowest waist of the part, the one a parallel jaw wants to close on and the one an unwanted gap lets it escape through. The **maximum width** is the diameter, and if the jaws cannot open that far there are orientations the gripper simply cannot reach around.

The part in this workshop is a chamfered aluminium bar, 60 mm long and 24 mm tall. Its diameter is not 60 mm, and reading why off the sweep is the point of the exercise.

lessons.title: A Cage Is Not a Grip
lessons.goal: Test whether a part can escape between two fingers by comparing the finger gap against the narrowest width of the part.
lessons.theory:
**Caging** is the weak cousin of form closure and it is more useful than it sounds. The object is free to move and rattle inside the fingers, but it cannot get out. A hook carrying a bucket cages it. A two finger gripper closing around a part before it touches it cages it first and grips it second.

The planar test is geometric. Two round fingers separated by a gap let the part through if, in **some** orientation, the part is narrower than the gap. So the part escapes when the narrowest width found in the last lesson is below the clear distance between the fingers, `narrowest(poly, angles)[0] < clear`, and `clear` is the centre distance minus one finger diameter because the fingers have bodies.

The consequence in the cell is a rule you can write down. Close the jaws to a gap under the narrowest width of the part **before** you move the wrist, and the part cannot leave even if the squeeze is zero and even if the vacuum in the next cell trips. Above it, the only thing holding the part is friction, and friction is the thing that fails.

The bar in the demonstration has a 24 mm waist and the fingers are 6 mm rods. Two gaps, two verdicts.

lessons.title: Facing Each Other Or Not
lessons.goal: Measure how far a pair of contacts is from being antipodal, in degrees.
lessons.theory:
A two finger grip wants its contacts **antipodal**: the segment joining them should run straight down both inward normals. When it does, the squeeze goes entirely into pressing the part and none of it into spinning the part out of the jaws.

Build the unit direction from the first contact to the second with `u = (p2 - p1) / np.linalg.norm(p2 - p1)`. A perfect pair has `n1` pointing along `u` and `n2` pointing along `-u`, so the honest score is the worse of the two angles, `max(angle_between(n1, u), angle_between(n2, -u))` in degrees. Zero is perfect, and anything past the friction angle you will meet in the next chapter is a grip that slides as soon as it closes.

Use the worse angle and not the average. An average hides the case where one pad is perfect and the other is 40 degrees off, which is exactly what happens when a jaw catches a chamfer, and that pair fails on the bad side no matter how good the other one is.

The three pairs in the demonstration are taken from the same bar: two flat faces, two chamfers, and one of each.

lessons.title: Firing a Ray Across the Part
lessons.goal: Find the contact on the far side of a part by casting a ray along the inward normal and keeping the nearest edge it hits.
lessons.theory:
You do not get contact pairs handed to you. You pick a point on the surface, fire a ray straight into the part along its inward normal, and whatever the ray leaves through is the other jaw. That is how every antipodal grasp sampler in the field generates candidates, and it is thirty lines.

The per edge intersection is already written for you as `hit_edge`, which returns the distance along the ray or `None` when that edge is not crossed. Your job is the selection: walk every edge, and when a hit comes back keep it only when it beats what you have, `if t is not None and (best_t is None or t < best_t):`. Inside that branch record both `best_t = t` and `best_i = i`, because the far contact needs the distance for its position and the edge index for its normal.

The exit point is then `origin + best_t * inward`, and the normal of the far contact is the inward normal of edge `best_i`. Convex parts always give exactly one exit, which is why the workshop keeps a convex hull of every part on file even when the part is not convex.

The demonstration fires from the middle of every edge of the bar and prints where each ray lands.

lessons.title: Which Line the Jaws Should Take
lessons.goal: Score every candidate contact pair on alignment and offset from the centre of mass, and pick the best one.
lessons.theory:
Now the two halves join. Fire rays from points along every edge, keep the pairs that come back, and you have a candidate list. Choosing among them is a ranking problem, and the ranking is where a grasp planner earns its keep.

Two penalties are enough at this stage. The first is the antipodal error in degrees from two lessons ago. The second is how far the midpoint of the grasp sits from the centre of mass, in millimetres, because a grip that is off centre has to fight a moment that a centred one never sees. Combine them as `error_deg + OFFSET_WEIGHT * offset_mm` and the weight sets the exchange rate: at `OFFSET_WEIGHT` of 2.0 one degree of misalignment costs as much as half a millimetre of offset.

Pick the winner with `min(scored, key=lambda item: item[0])` and print the top of the list, not only the winner. One warning about reading that list: every physical grasp appears in it **twice**, once fired from each of its two contacts, so the first two rows being an exact tie is the same pair of jaws seen from both ends and not two options. Look at rank three for the first real alternative.

The centre of mass comes from the shoelace centroid of the polygon, not from the middle of the bounding box. For this chamfered bar the difference is 1.5 mm upward, and it moves the ranking.
lessons.task: Fill in `score(candidate)` with the weighted penalty and `best(scored)` with the selection, then read the ranked list.

lessons.title: The Angle Friction Allows
lessons.goal: Convert a friction coefficient into a friction cone half angle and into the tangential force a squeeze buys.
lessons.theory:
Form closure is rare in a real cell. Almost everything a robot picks is held by friction, and friction has exactly one parameter that matters at this level: the coefficient `mu` between the pad and the part.

It buys two things and it is worth seeing both. As a **force**, the largest tangential load a contact can carry before sliding is `mu * normal_force`, so a 30 N squeeze through a nitrile pad at 0.8 carries 24 N sideways. As an **angle**, it says how far from the normal a contact force is allowed to lean, `math.degrees(math.atan(mu))`, which is the half angle of the **friction cone**. Everything in this chapter is that cone.

The numbers are humbler than people expect. Bare steel jaws on an oiled steel part sit near 0.15, which is 8.5 degrees of freedom to lean. Nitrile on dry aluminium is about 0.8, or 38.7 degrees. That difference is not a detail, it is the difference between a gripper that works and one that needs three times the force and crushes the part.

And `mu` is not a constant. It drops with a film of coolant, it drops as the pad polishes, and the number on the datasheet was measured dry on a clean sample.

lessons.title: Inside the Cone or Sliding

lessons.theory:
A contact force is **feasible** when two things hold at once, and code that checks only the second one is the classic bug.

First, the normal component has to be positive. A pad pushes; it does not pull. A solver that returns a negative normal force has quietly attached the part to the finger with glue and the answer it gives you is fiction.

Second, the tangential magnitude has to fit under the cone. Split the force the way you did in the opening chapter: `fn` is the normal component and `ft = float(np.linalg.norm(f - fn * n))` is what is left. The contact sticks while `fn > 0.0 and ft <= mu * fn`, and slides otherwise.

The three forces in the demonstration are the three cases you will meet: a clean push well inside the cone, a push leaning too far to hold, and a force with a negative normal component that some optimiser was happy to hand you. The second and third fail for completely different reasons, and your log line should say which.

lessons.title: How Hard to Squeeze
lessons.goal: Size the normal force two pads need to hold a hanging part, and check it against what the part survives.
lessons.theory:
Here is the calculation that decides whether a pick is possible at all. A part hangs between two pads. Each pad carries at most `mu` times its normal force sideways, and between them they have to carry the weight, so the smallest squeeze that works is `mass * G / (2.0 * mu)` newtons.

So the pick has two walls: below the minimum it slides, above the crush limit it breaks, and if those two cross there is no squeeze that works and the answer is a different pad or a different gripper.

lessons.title: The Cone Has Edges
lessons.goal: Approximate a three dimensional friction cone with a set of edge vectors that a linear solver can use.
lessons.theory:
The friction cone is round, and round is inconvenient. Every practical grasp solver replaces it with a pyramid: a handful of **edge vectors**, and any nonnegative combination of them is a force the solver is allowed to use. The answer becomes slightly conservative, because the pyramid sits inside the cone, and in exchange the whole problem turns linear.

Building the edges needs a pair of unit vectors spanning the tangent plane, and `tangent_basis(n)` is written for you. Then walk the circle: at step `k` of `edges` the angle is `a = 2.0 * math.pi * k / edges` and the edge vector is `n + mu * (math.cos(a) * t1 + math.sin(a) * t2)`. The normal part has length one and the tangential part has length `mu`, so each edge leans exactly the friction angle away from the normal, which is the definition you want.

Four edges is the usual cheap choice and it keeps about 71 percent of the true cone at the worst azimuth. Eight edges keeps 92 percent. More than that rarely changes a verdict and always costs solver time.

The demonstration builds the edges for a nitrile pad and measures the lean of each one back against `math.atan(mu)`, which is how you catch a tangent basis that is not orthonormal.

lessons.title: Soft Fingers Twist Too
lessons.goal: Add a torsional friction limit to a contact and show why a point fingertip cannot resist a twist at all.
lessons.theory:
A hard fingertip touching a flat face is a **point contact with friction**: it resists a push and a slide and nothing else. Spin the part about the contact normal and the fingertip offers no resistance, because a point has no area to generate a moment over.

A soft pad is a different animal, and it is what your gripper actually has. It flattens against the part into a patch of radius `radius`, and the friction spread over that patch resists a twist. The standard model is the **soft finger contact**, which adds one number, a torsional coefficient `mu_t = 0.6 * mu * radius`, in metres, and the largest twist the contact holds is that coefficient times the normal force.

The two limits are not independent. Sliding sideways uses up the same friction that resisting the twist needs, and the accepted approximation is an ellipse: the contact holds while `(ft / (mu * fn)) ** 2 + (tz / (mu_t * fn)) ** 2 <= 1.0`. Spend it all on the slide and you have nothing left for the twist.

The demonstration puts the same 4 N slide and 0.020 Nm twist on a 1 mm hard tip and on an 8 mm silicone pad, at the same 8 N squeeze. One of the two is not close.

lessons.title: The Line Has to Fit in Both Cones
lessons.goal: Give a two finger force closure verdict by comparing the antipodal error against the friction angle.
lessons.theory:
For two fingers in the plane there is a force closure test you can do in your head, and it joins the two halves of this course.

If the segment joining the contacts lies inside **both** friction cones, the fingers can squeeze along that line and generate any force the part needs without sliding. If it leans outside either cone, the squeeze itself makes the part slip out. So the verdict is `antipodal_error(p1, n1, p2, n2) <= friction_angle(mu)`, using the same error function from the first chapter, and the useful number to log alongside it is the margin, `friction_angle(mu) - antipodal_error(p1, n1, p2, n2)`, in degrees.

This is why a perfectly aligned pair is worth chasing. At zero error the pair holds with any friction at all, even a polished steel jaw at 0.15. At 28 degrees of error you need a pad that leans 28 degrees, which is `mu` above 0.53, and a steel jaw simply cannot do it no matter how hard you squeeze.

Squeezing harder never fixes alignment. The cone is an angle, and an angle does not care about newtons. That single sentence saves more parts than any controller in this course.

lessons.title: The Matrix the Fingers Speak Through
lessons.goal: Build the planar grasp matrix that maps a stack of contact forces to the wrench on the object.
lessons.theory:
Two fingers with a hand test is fine. Three fingers, or four, or a hand with a thumb, needs the general machinery, and the general machinery is one matrix.

The **grasp matrix** `G` takes the contact forces stacked into one long vector and returns the wrench they produce on the object. Each contact contributes a block of two columns in the plane, one per force component, and the block is `np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [-r[1], r[0]]])`: the force passes straight through to the force rows, and the bottom row is the moment the lever arm makes. Write the block into its slot with `G[:, 2 * i:2 * i + 2] = block` and you are done.

Once `G` exists the questions get short. `G @ forces` is the wrench the hand is applying. A wrench you want is a linear system in `forces`. The null space of `G`, which is the next lesson, is every way of changing the finger forces without the object noticing.

The demonstration builds `G` for a two finger grip on the bar and feeds it three force vectors: a pure squeeze, an even lift, and a lift where one pad pulls up while the other pulls down. Only the third one produces a moment, and reading which row it lands in is the check that your block is the right way round.

lessons.title: Can It Fight Any Push
lessons.goal: Decide force closure by checking that every sampled wrench direction has at least one cone edge pushing against it.
lessons.theory:
The general force closure question is: can the fingers produce **every** wrench, in every direction, using only forces inside their cones? There is a linear program for it and there is a sampling test, and the sampling test is the one you can write today and debug tomorrow.

Stack the cone edges of every contact as columns of wrenches. The fingers can only produce nonnegative combinations of those columns. That positive span misses some direction exactly when there is a unit wrench `d` with every column pointing away from it, so the test per direction is `max(float(np.dot(w, d)) for w in columns) > 0.0`, and the grasp is force closure when `all(resists(columns, d) for d in directions)`.

The same units trap as the twist sampler applies, and the sampler here scales the moment row by the part radius so a newton metre and a newton are comparable. Get that wrong and the test blesses grasps that spin the part out.

lessons.title: The Squeeze That Costs Nothing
lessons.goal: Find the null space of the grasp matrix and show that squeezing harder changes the contact forces without changing the object wrench.
lessons.theory:
Two fingers pressing on opposite sides of a part with 5 N each, and the same two fingers pressing with 50 N each, apply exactly the same wrench to the object: none. That difference lives in the **null space** of the grasp matrix, and it has a name, the **internal force**, or in shop language the squeeze.

It is the most useful degree of freedom in the hand. It does not move the part, so it is free from the point of view of the task, and it is the only knob that keeps the contacts inside their friction cones. Every grasp force controller in existence is choosing a point in this null space.

Get it out of a singular value decomposition. Take `_, s, vt = np.linalg.svd(G)`, count the nonzero singular values with `rank = int(np.sum(s > 1e-9))`, and the rows of `vt` from `rank` onwards are an orthonormal basis of the null space, so `return vt[rank:]` hands them back.

The demonstration adds 20 N of the internal direction to a working grasp. The object wrench does not move. The normal force at each pad does, and that is the number the next chapters spend their time on.

A planner produces hundreds of candidate grasps and has to sort them. Sorting needs a number, and the cheapest honest number comes straight out of the grasp matrix.

The singular values of `G` say how much object wrench you get per unit of finger force, direction by direction. lessons.title: The Direction It Is Weakest In
lessons.goal: Read the left singular vector of the smallest singular value and name the wrench direction the grasp resists worst.
lessons.theory:
A score tells you that a grasp is weak. The singular vector tells you **what** it is weak against, and that is the part you can act on.

The full decomposition returns three things, `u, s, _ = np.linalg.svd(G)`, and the columns of `u` are directions in wrench space. The column belonging to the smallest singular value is the wrench direction the fingers can barely produce: find its index with `k = int(np.argmin(s))` and hand back both halves with `return u[:, k], float(s[k])`. Its three entries are a force along x, a force along y and a moment, in the scaled units of this chapter, so you can read it as a sentence.

For the wide pair across the bar that vector comes out as pure moment. That is not a bug and it is not fixable by squeezing: two point contacts on a line have nothing to push with against a twist about that line, which is exactly the escape the very first chapter found by sampling twists. Two chapters, two methods, same answer.

For the narrow pair the weak direction mixes a lift with a moment, which is the signature of two fingers too close together on one face. When a grasp fails on the cell floor, this vector usually says why before the video does.

lessons.title: The Same in Every Direction
lessons.goal: Compute the isotropy and the condition number of a grasp and say what each one is good for.
lessons.theory:
The smallest singular value is an absolute capacity, and it changes if you double every finger force. Sometimes you want the **shape** of the capacity instead of its size, and that is a ratio.

**Isotropy** is `float(s.min() / s.max())`, between zero and one, and one means the grasp is equally effective in every wrench direction. **Condition number** is the same information upside down, `float(s.max() / s.min())`, starting at one and running to infinity. Roboticists quote whichever makes their grasp look better, which is a reason to compute both and put them next to each other.

Use isotropy when you are comparing grasps for a task whose wrench direction you do not know, which is the usual case in a bin. Use the smallest singular value when you do know it, because a grasp can be beautifully isotropic and uniformly feeble.

The demonstration will show you something that surprises people: the plain two finger pair across the bar is perfectly isotropic, better than the tripod. That is true and it is also not a reason to prefer it, which is what the next two lessons are about.

lessons.title: The Largest Push It Always Survives
lessons.goal: Compute the epsilon quality of a grasp as the smallest support of its cone wrenches over all directions.
lessons.theory:
The metric the field actually ranks grasps on is geometric: how big a ball of wrenches, centred on the origin, fits inside everything the fingers can produce? Its radius is called the **epsilon quality**, and it answers the only question that matters on the floor, which is how hard the world can push before the part moves.

You already have the machinery. The cone edges of every contact are the wrenches the fingers can produce, and for one direction `d` the best the hand can do against it is `max(float(np.dot(w, d)) for w in columns)`, the support of the set. The radius of the largest ball is then the worst of those over every direction, `min(support(columns, d) for d in directions)`.

A positive epsilon is force closure with a margin. A zero means the grasp is exactly on the boundary. A negative one names a direction the hand cannot fight at all, and the magnitude says how badly. That last case is the useful one: a planner that prints minus 0.78 is telling you the grasp is not marginal, it is hopeless.

The demonstration runs the three layouts through a nitrile pad. Compare the ranking with the singular value ranking of three lessons ago, because they do not agree.

lessons.title: The Metric That Cannot See Friction
lessons.goal: Show that two grasps with identical grasp matrices have opposite epsilon qualities, and say which metric to trust.
lessons.theory:
Here is a test worth running on any metric before you ship it: delete the thing the metric is supposed to measure and see whether the number moves.

The grasp matrix is built from contact **positions** only. Nowhere in it does a contact normal appear. So take a working two finger grasp and rotate both normals 28 degrees, leaving the contacts exactly where they are. The grasp matrix is byte for byte the same. Every singular value is the same. The epsilon quality sees it immediately, because the cone edges are built from the normals. Rank on epsilon, or on anything that consumes the normals and `mu`. Use the singular values for what they are good at, which is telling you that finger placement is degenerate before you spend three thousand dot products finding out.

Read the demonstration as a pair of columns. One column is identical top to bottom and proves the metric is blind. The other changes sign.

lessons.title: How Close Each Finger Is to Sliding
lessons.goal: Solve the contact forces for a task wrench, add internal force, and report the cone margin of every finger.
lessons.theory:
Epsilon scores the grasp against every possible wrench. Once you know the wrench the task actually needs, there is a sharper question: with the forces the hand is really applying, how much room does each finger have left?

Solve the forces first. `np.linalg.lstsq` on the physical grasp matrix gives the minimum norm force set that produces the target wrench, and the physical matrix here is the unscaled one, because these are newtons and you want newtons back. That solution is almost always outside the cones, because least squares has no idea cones exist, and the fix is the internal direction from the second chapter: add squeeze until the fingers are inside.

The margin of a contact is `mu * fn - ft`, the tangential capacity it has not spent. Negative means sliding right now. The grasp margin is `min(margins)`, because the first finger to let go decides.

The demonstration holds a 600 g part with a lift wrench and sweeps the squeeze from zero. At zero squeeze the least squares answer is asking the pads to carry the whole weight in friction with no normal force at all, which is the classic solver output that looks fine in a plot and drops the part.

lessons.goal: Compare the moment an off centre grasp has to resist against the moment two pads can generate.
lessons.theory:
Grip a 60 mm bar 30 mm off its centre of mass, accelerate it, and the part tries to rotate in the jaws. Nothing about the friction coefficient stops that; what stops it is the pair of pads being far enough apart to make a couple.

The demand side is a lever: `mass * accel * offset` newton metres, where `accel` is the worst acceleration in the move, not the average, and where a 2 g transport is normal for a fast cell. The supply side is the couple two pads can make, `2.0 * mu * fn * halfspan`, one tangential force at each pad acting at half the grasp span.

Both sides are linear in the things you can change, which makes the trade obvious. Doubling the squeeze doubles the supply. Doubling the offset doubles the demand. Halving the grasp span halves the supply, which is why a narrow pinch on a long part is a bad idea even when the friction numbers are comfortable.

The demonstration holds the bar at 8 N per pad and walks the grasp point out from the centre of mass. Read where the two curves cross, then remember that in a real cell the offset comes from a vision estimate you do not fully trust.

lessons.title: Fingers Too Close Together
lessons.goal: Measure the area of the triangle three fingers make and reject a layout that has collapsed onto a line.
lessons.theory:
A three finger hand has a cheap sanity check that catches the worst layouts before any decomposition runs: the area of the triangle the contacts make.

In the plane it is one determinant, `0.5 * abs(cross2(b - a, c - a))`, in square metres, and `cross2` is the two dimensional cross product written out for you because `np.cross` on two dimensional vectors is deprecated and will stop working. It is small when the fingers bunch up, and it is exactly zero when they land on a line, which is the case the rank test of the first chapter also catches and which a sampler produces more often than you would like on a flat part.

So the filter is `area >= MIN_AREA`, and picking `MIN_AREA` is a judgement about your part, not a universal constant. Two hundred square millimetres is a sane floor for a 60 mm part, and the rule of thumb behind it is that the contacts should span something like a third of the part in each direction.

Run it first in a pipeline. It costs one cross product per candidate and it removes the layouts that would otherwise waste a full epsilon evaluation and come back at minus something.

A planner cannot act on four numbers. At the end of the chapter they collapse into one, and the collapse is a design decision you should write down rather than tune until the demo works.

lessons.title: The Pose Before the Pose
lessons.goal: Build the pre grasp and retreat poses from a grasp pose, a standoff and a lift height.
lessons.theory:
A pick is never one pose. It is at least three, and skipping the other two is how a gripper knocks a part over on the way in.

The **pre grasp** sits back along the approach axis by a standoff, `grasp - standoff * approach`, where `approach` is the unit vector the gripper travels along. Fifty millimetres is a normal standoff for a 2F-85, and it exists so that everything between the pre grasp and the grasp is a straight line the planner does not have to think about.

The **retreat** is the pose the gripper goes to once the jaws are closed, and it goes straight up, `grasp + LIFT * np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])`, before any lateral motion. Straight up, not along the approach axis backwards: a part that just came out of a fixture is still surrounded by the fixture, and up is the only direction guaranteed to be empty.

The three poses together are the shape of every pick in this workshop, and the rest of the chapter is what happens between them.

lessons.goal: Interpolate the approach into waypoints and verify that no single step is longer than the servo can track.
lessons.theory:
A straight line between two poses is a plan, not a trajectory. The controller wants waypoints, and the spacing of those waypoints is a safety property: a 50 mm jump commanded to a position servo becomes a lunge, and the part is gone before the force sensor has a chance to say anything.

Interpolating is one expression. lessons.title: The Neighbours Get a Vote
lessons.goal: Reject a grasp whose open fingers would strike a neighbouring part before the pads reach the target.
lessons.theory:
In a bin the target is not alone. The jaws have to fit into the gap around it, and a grasp that is perfect in isolation is worthless if a neighbouring part sits where a finger has to go.

The subtlety is which fingers to test. Test the **open** positions, not the closed ones, because the fingers arrive open and close afterwards. A planner that checks the closed jaw passes grasps that collide on the way in, and the failure looks like a random knock rather than a planning bug.

A parallel jaw grasp does not care which finger goes on which side, so the grasp axis gives you an angle and that angle plus 180 degrees, and both are correct grasps. The wrist cares very much, because one of them may be past a joint limit and one of them may need a 300 degree unwind.

lessons.goal: Shape the approach speed so the last centimetres are travelled at creep speed with a linear ramp above it.
lessons.theory:
Speed on approach is a trade you make twice. Far from the part, fast is free. Near the part, fast is the difference between detecting contact at 3 N and detecting it at 40 N, because the force you measure is the speed you were carrying when you hit.

The profile has three pieces and one of them is the important one. Inside `CREEP_DISTANCE`, which is 10 mm here, the speed is fixed at `CREEP_SPEED`. Above it the speed ramps linearly: `ratio = min(1.0, (distance - CREEP_DISTANCE) / RAMP_LENGTH)` says how far up the ramp you are, and the speed is `CREEP_SPEED + ratio * (FAST_SPEED - CREEP_SPEED)`. Past the top of the ramp the `min` pins it at the fast speed and no branch is needed.

The reason to ramp rather than to step is not comfort. A step in commanded speed is a step in commanded acceleration, and on an arm with any compliance in the last link that shows up as a wobble at exactly the moment you are trying to read a small force.

The demonstration prints the profile from 100 mm out and confirms the creep speed is really reached before contact.

lessons.title: Moving Until Something Pushes Back
lessons.goal: Implement a guarded move that steps down until the measured force crosses a threshold, and measure the overshoot it leaves.
lessons.theory:
The surface is never where the model says it is. A **guarded move** solves that by not caring: command small steps towards the surface and stop when the force sensor says you have arrived.

The loop is short. Step, read the force, and `if force >= FORCE_THRESHOLD:` record `contact_z = z` and break. The simulated environment here is a stiff surface that pushes back proportionally to how far you have pressed into it, which is a reasonable model of a machined fixture and a terrible model of foam.

The number worth staring at is the **overshoot**: the distance between where contact actually happened and where you stopped. It is never zero, because you only find out after the step that took you in, so it is bounded below by the step size and made worse by any delay in the force reading. That is the same reason the last lesson slowed the approach down.

The demonstration runs the identical guarded move at a 2 mm step and at a 0.5 mm step. The stopping heights differ, the peak forces differ by a factor of four, and neither run knew where the surface was.

lessons.title: Leaving Is Also a Path
lessons.goal: Build the traverse of a retreat from the top of the lift and check that the carried part clears the bin wall.
lessons.theory:
More parts are lost on the way out than on the way in. The gripper is holding something now, the something hangs below the jaws, and the bin wall is exactly at the height the operator finds convenient.

The retreat is two segments and only one of them needs checking. The vertical segment is safe by construction: it retraces the approach the gripper just came down, and nothing has moved except the part now in the jaws. So the path you build starts at the top of that lift, `top = np.array([start[0], start[1], start[2] + lift])`, and the traverse is sampled from there rather than assumed, because a straight line between two safe poses is not a safe line.

The check is a swept one, and it is done on the bottom of the **part**, not on the tool centre, because the part hangs `PART_DROP` below the jaws. For every sampled point still over the bin, meaning `abs(p[0]) <= WALL_X`, it has to clear: `all(p[2] > WALL_HEIGHT + CLEARANCE for p in bottoms if abs(p[0]) <= WALL_X)`.

The demonstration runs the same retreat with two lift heights over a 120 mm wall. One of them drags the part along the rim for the first part of the traverse, which in a real cell you hear before you see.

lessons.title: Stroke, Pads and What Fits
lessons.goal: Decide whether a part fits a parallel jaw gripper once the pad thickness and the approach gap are counted.
lessons.theory:
A 2F-85 opens 85 mm, and the largest part it picks is nowhere near 85 mm wide. Two 6 mm pads eat 12 mm of that, and you want a couple of millimetres either side so the fingers do not scrape the part on the way in.

So the opening test is `width + 2.0 * (PAD_THICKNESS + APPROACH_GAP) <= MAX_OPENING`, which on this gripper leaves 65 mm of real capacity out of a headline 85. Write that expression once, in the place that decides pickability, rather than remembering to subtract by hand at three call sites.

The other end of the range is quieter and catches people out. A parallel jaw has a minimum useful width too, `width >= MIN_GRIP_WIDTH`, because below it the pads meet before they touch the part and the drive stalls against itself. On a 2F-85 with these pads that floor is around 4 mm, and a bare terminal pin is under it.

The demonstration runs four parts from the workshop bench through both tests. Two fit, and the two that do not fail at opposite ends of the range.

lessons.title: Current Is the Only Force Sensor You Have
lessons.goal: Turn a gripper motor current into an estimated jaw force and mark the readings that are below the noise floor.
lessons.theory:
Most industrial grippers have no force sensor. What they have is a motor, and the current that motor draws is roughly proportional to the force at the jaws once the drivetrain is loaded. That is the whole force feedback path on a cell that costs a hundred thousand euros.

The conversion has an offset because the motor draws current to move itself before it touches anything: `FORCE_PER_AMP * max(0.0, current - NO_LOAD_CURRENT)`. The `max` is not decoration. Without it a jaw closing on empty air reports a negative force, and a comparison somewhere downstream will be delighted by that.

The second half is knowing when to believe the number. Just above the no load current the estimate is mostly friction in the screw and it moves with temperature, so mark a reading as trustworthy only while `current > NO_LOAD_CURRENT + DEADBAND`. Below that band you know the jaw is not pushing hard; you do not know how hard.

The demonstration sweeps the current from idle to stall on a gripper with a 55 N per amp constant. Read where the trusted flag turns on, and remember that the whole band below it is where a delicate part would be held.

lessons.title: The Window Between Slipping and Cracking
lessons.goal: Command a grip force inside the window between the friction minimum and the crush limit, and refuse when the window is empty.
lessons.theory:
Two chapters ago you computed the smallest squeeze that holds a part, and the largest squeeze the part survives. A gripper driver has to turn those two numbers into one command, or into an honest refusal.

The floor is `lo = SAFETY * mass * G / (2.0 * mu)`, the friction minimum with the safety factor already applied. The ceiling is the crush limit off the part datasheet or off a test with a load cell and three sacrificial parts. lessons.title: The Cup Holds Because Air Pushes
lessons.goal: Size a vacuum cup by turning its diameter and its vacuum level into a holding force.
lessons.theory:
A suction cup does not pull. The atmosphere pushes, and the cup simply removes some of the air on one side so the push stops being balanced. That framing makes the arithmetic obvious and stops people believing a cup can exceed one atmosphere.

The area is the sealing area, `math.pi * (0.5 * cup_diameter) ** 2`, and the vacuum level is how far below atmospheric you pulled it, in kilopascals, so the force is `vacuum_kpa * 1000.0 * area / VACUUM_SAFETY`. A shop system reaching minus 60 kPa on a 30 mm cup gives about 42 N before the safety factor and about 21 N after it, which is a 2 kg part in clean lift and a good deal less in practice.

The safety factor is not optional and it is not 1.5 because someone was nervous. Cups leak, the vacuum sags when the ejector shares a manifold with another station, the seal creeps on a warm part, and the part is rarely lifted straight up.

The demonstration sizes three standard cups against the same 1.2 kg sheet and reports which ones hold it, which is exactly the sheet you fill in when specifying an end effector.

lessons.title: Shear Is Not Lift
lessons.goal: Find the largest tilt a vacuum cup can carry a part at, given that shear is limited by friction and not by vacuum.
lessons.theory:
The number on a cup datasheet is a lift rating, measured straight down the cup axis. Tilt the part and the load splits, and the two halves are limited by completely different physics.

The part of the weight along the cup axis is `weight * math.cos(math.radians(tilt))`, and that is what the vacuum resists directly. The part in the plane of the seal is shear, and vacuum does nothing about shear at all: what holds it is friction between the rubber and the part, so the test is `shear <= MU_CUP * hold`. With a cup friction coefficient around 0.5, a cup rated for 20 N of lift holds only 10 N sideways.

The consequence is a rule for placing cups, not a rule for sizing them. Put the cup on the face whose normal points along the load, and if the part must be carried tilted, size the cup for the shear case and not for the lift case. Handling systems that pick sheets flat and stack them vertically live entirely in this inequality.

The demonstration sweeps the tilt of a 1.2 kg sheet on a 30 mm cup and prints the crossing angle up front so you can see which of the two limits the sweep runs into. It is the shear one, and it arrives long before the vacuum runs out.

lessons.title: Cardboard Leaks
lessons.goal: Model the vacuum decaying through a leaking seal and compute how long the cup can still hold the part.
lessons.theory:
A cup on machined aluminium seals. A cup on corrugated cardboard leaks through the flutes, and on a system with a small pump the vacuum starts falling the moment the ejector cycles off.

A first order decay is close enough to plan with: `level = level * math.exp(-DT / time_constant)`, where the time constant is a property of the leak and the reservoir together, not of the cup alone. Sealed steel gives tens of seconds. Single wall cardboard gives two or three. Foam packaging gives less than one and should not be picked with a cup at all.

What you want out of the model is a **time budget**: the moment when `hold_force(level) < required` first becomes true. Everything from grasp to release has to happen inside it, and if your traverse takes four seconds and the budget is two, the answer is a bigger reservoir or a different tool, not a faster arm.

The demonstration runs the same 1.2 kg part on a sealed surface and on cardboard, and prints the second at which each one lets go. Only one of them lets go inside the ten seconds simulated, which is the point.

lessons.title: One Motor, Two Knuckles
lessons.goal: Split the tendon tension of an underactuated finger between its two phalanges and detect the ratio that ejects the part.
lessons.theory:
An underactuated finger has two joints and one motor. A tendon runs over a pulley at each joint, and the finger closes around whatever shape it meets without any sensing. That is why fruit picking hands and prosthetic hands are built this way, and why they occasionally throw the object out of the hand.

The torques come straight off the pulley radii: `tau1 = tension * radius1` at the proximal joint and `tau2 = tension * radius2` at the distal one. The contact forces follow from the transmission. The distal phalanx sees `f2 = tau2 / LENGTH2` and the proximal one sees whatever torque is left after the distal joint took its share, `f1 = (tau1 - tau2) / LENGTH1`.

That subtraction is the whole story. Make the distal pulley too large relative to the proximal one and `f1` goes **negative**, which means the proximal phalanx is no longer pushing on the part. The finger has rolled onto its tip, and a negative `f1` in your model is a part launched out of the hand in the workshop.

The demonstration runs the same 40 N tendon through two pulley ratios. Read the sign of `f1` in each.

lessons.title: The Pad Flattens Under Load
lessons.goal: Compute the contact patch a compliant pad makes on a round part and turn it into torsional grip capacity.
lessons.theory:
The soft finger contact of the second chapter needed a patch radius and you were handed one. It is not a constant: it grows with the squeeze, which means the twist a grip resists grows with the squeeze twice over, once through the normal force and once through the patch.

Model the pad as a linear spring, so it compresses `d = force / PAD_STIFFNESS` metres under load. The demonstration sweeps the squeeze on a 60 shore pad against a 20 mm shaft. Compare the growth of the patch against the growth of the twist capacity, and note that the pad model stops being honest once the compression approaches the pad thickness.

Everything so far assumed a gripper was already bolted on. Choosing it is a decision that a short ordered rule chain makes better than a long argument, provided the order is written down and defended.

The chain here is three tests and a default. `if porous:` comes first, because a cup on cardboard or foam is a leak whatever else is true, and the last lesson but one showed what that costs. lessons.theory:
A position controller has one job and it does it without judgement: go to the commanded pose and stay there. When the commanded pose is inside a solid object, staying there means pushing as hard as the arm can push.

The fix for the last lesson is not a better position controller. It is a controller that behaves like a **spring** instead of like a vice, so that a position error turns into a bounded force rather than an unbounded one.

The spring is virtual and you choose it. Given a force you are willing to apply and the position error you expect to have, the stiffness that connects them is `k = target_force / position_error`. lessons.title: Damping the Bounce Out
lessons.goal: Add damping to a virtual spring, sweep the damping ratio, and measure the overshoot each one leaves.
lessons.theory:
A spring on its own oscillates forever. Add a virtual damper and the second order system you have built gets the behaviour you asked for, which is arriving once rather than seven times.

The damping constant that goes with a stiffness and a moving mass is `2.0 * zeta * math.sqrt(stiffness * mass)`, where `zeta` is the damping ratio and one means critically damped. The force on the tool is then `force = -STIFFNESS * (x - x_ref) - b * v`, the spring pulling towards the reference and the damper opposing whatever speed the tool has, and integrating that twice is the whole simulation.

Three ratios matter in practice. Under 0.4 the tool bounces, and every bounce is a force spike against whatever it landed on. Around 0.7 it overshoots once by a few percent and settles fastest, which is why it is the default in almost every impedance controller shipped. Above 1.2 it never overshoots and arrives late, which is what you want when the thing it is approaching is fragile and slow is acceptable.

The demonstration runs 0.8 seconds, which is eight natural periods at this stiffness, because a window of one or two periods makes an underdamped system look settled. It reports the overshoot past the reference and the moment the tool last leaves a 0.2 mm band around it, which is the number that shows why 0.7 is the default: it settles in a fifth of the time the overdamped run needs, and in a seventh of what the bouncy one needs.

lessons.title: Impedance Does Not Regulate Force

lessons.theory:
Here is the thing about impedance control that catches people who expected a force controller. It does not control force. It controls the **relation** between position error and force, and the force you end up with depends entirely on how far past the surface you told it to go.

The settling force is the virtual spring stretched by the difference between the commanded position and the real surface, so it is `STIFFNESS * (surface_z - x_ref)` once the motion stops. Command 3 mm past a surface with a 2500 newton per metre stiffness and you get 7.5 N. Move the surface 2 mm without telling the controller and you get 2.5 N or 12.5 N, and nothing in the loop notices.

The environment stiffness barely matters for the settling value, which is the useful half of the property: the same command gives roughly the same force on foam and on steel, as long as the environment is much stiffer than your virtual spring. That is exactly the robustness the first lesson of this chapter was missing.

lessons.title: Admittance Is the Other Way Round
lessons.goal: Implement an admittance update and show that the gain that behaves on foam diverges on steel.
lessons.theory:
Impedance reads position and writes force. **Admittance** reads force and writes position, which is what you do when the arm underneath you only accepts position commands, and that is most industrial arms.

The update is one line: `x_ref = x_ref + (f_desired - f_measured) / K_ADM`, where `K_ADM` is an admittance gain in newtons per metre. Push too hard and the reference backs off. Push too little and it advances. It is a proportional controller in disguise, and its loop gain is not what you set, it is what you set **divided by the environment**.

Work the arithmetic out and it is exact. With a perfect position servo the force error next cycle is the current error times `1 - K_ENV / K_ADM`. That converges while the ratio stays under two and diverges above it, and `K_ENV` is a property of whatever the robot happened to touch. So a gain tuned on a foam nest at 5000 newtons per metre, with a comfortable ratio of a third, meets a steel fixture at 40000 and gets a ratio of 2.7.

The demonstration runs the identical controller on both. The foam run walks onto 5 N and stays. The steel run never settles: it slams to two and a half times the target, bounces clear of the surface entirely, comes back, and repeats. In a cell that is the buzzing you hear when somebody tunes an admittance loop on the wrong fixture.

lessons.title: Asking For a Force and Getting It
lessons.goal: Close a proportional integral loop on force error with a clamped integrator and show the offset the integral removes.
lessons.theory:
Impedance gives you a spring and its force depends on where the surface is. Closing a loop on the force error itself fixes that, and the loop is a standard PI whose output is a **position offset** into the surface.

Proportional alone cannot get there and the arithmetic says why. The force produced is the environment stiffness times the offset, so `f = K_ENV * KP * (F_DESIRED - f)`, and solving that leaves a permanent error of the target divided by one plus `K_ENV * KP`. With the gains in this file that leaves it resting at 3.506 N against a target of 8, sitting there forever, and no amount of patience closes it.

The integral term is what eats it, and it is also what breaks a cell when it is left unbounded, so it goes in clamped: `integral = min(I_LIMIT, max(-I_LIMIT, integral + error * DT))`. The command that comes out is `offset = KP * error + KI * integral`, in metres, and the reference is placed that far inside the nominal surface.

The demonstration runs the same contact with the integral term switched on and off, for three seconds. The proportional only run is flat from the first cycle and stays flat, and its resting value is exactly what the formula above predicts.

lessons.title: Losing Contact Is a Bug
lessons.goal: Show a force integrator winding up while the tool is in free air and add the guard that stops the slam on re contact.
lessons.theory:
A force controller in free air is asking for a force nothing is providing. The error sits at the full target, the integrator accumulates every cycle of it until it hits its clamp, and the reference sinks into a surface that is not there. Then the part arrives and everything the integrator saved up is spent in one hit.

This is the single most common failure of a first force controller, and it does not show up in the tuning session, because during tuning the tool is already touching something. It shows up the first time a part is missing from the fixture.

The guard is three lines. Name the condition, `in_contact = force >= CONTACT_THRESHOLD`, with a threshold above your sensor noise. Then `if guarded and not in_contact:` clear the integrator. Some implementations also freeze the reference where it is, which is better still, but clearing the integrator is what removes the slam.

The demonstration drops the surface out from under the controller for a second and puts it back. Compare the peak force on re contact between the two runs, and note that the unguarded peak is set by `I_LIMIT` rather than by anything physical: raise the clamp and the peak rises with it.

lessons.title: Position Here, Force There
lessons.goal: Split a Cartesian command with a selection matrix so one axis tracks position while another regulates force.
lessons.theory:
Wiping a surface, deburring an edge, seating a connector: all of them want position control along some axes and force control along others, at the same time. **Hybrid control** does that with a diagonal selection matrix and no cleverness at all.

Build the selection as a vector of ones and zeros, `selection = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])` for a task that regulates force along z and position along x and y. Then blend the two commands with `(1.0 - selection) * position_cmd + selection * force_cmd`, which takes each axis from exactly one controller. The two controllers never fight, because no axis is ever driven by both.

The part that goes wrong is the frame. The selection is expressed in the **task** frame, not the base frame, and a surface tilted 20 degrees needs the selection rotated with it, or the force controller pushes partly along the surface and the position controller tries to drive into it. That rotation is where the bugs live.

The demonstration wipes 100 mm across a surface while closing on 6 N against it. Read the x command, which never changes because nothing on that axis is negotiable, next to the z command, which shrinks as the force error closes.

lessons.title: The Torque the Joints Have to Make
lessons.goal: Map a desired fingertip force into joint torques through the Jacobian transpose and check them against the motor ratings.
lessons.theory:
All of this chapter has been asking for forces at the fingertip. The motors do not make forces, they make torques, and the bridge between the two is the transpose of the Jacobian you built in the Joint Cathedral.

The relation is `tau = J.T @ f`, and it is exact, not an approximation. It falls out of equating the work done at the tip with the work done at the joints, so it holds at every configuration including the singular ones. Note that it needs the **transpose** and not the inverse, which is why static force mapping is the well behaved half of manipulator statics: nothing here divides by anything.

The check that goes with it is `np.all(np.abs(tau) <= LIMITS)`, per joint, against the continuous rating rather than the peak rating if the push lasts longer than a second. Failing it is not a reason to reduce the force blindly; often it is a reason to change the configuration, because the same tip force costs wildly different torques depending on where the arm is folded.

The demonstration pushes 30 N in two directions at two configurations of a 2R arm. The combination that fails is the extended arm pushed sideways, where the whole reach acts as a lever on the shoulder. The same 30 N through the folded arm costs the shoulder about a third less, which is a planning decision and not a gripper one.

lessons.theory:
A tactile pad is a grid of pressure cells, sixteen of them on a modest fingertip and several hundred on a research one. Nothing downstream wants a grid. What the grasp controller wants is two numbers.

lessons.title: The Contact Walked
lessons.goal: Detect slip from the drift of the centre of pressure across a window, and see why consecutive frames cannot do it.
lessons.theory:
When a part slips through the fingers, the contact patch does not stay where it was. The centre of pressure walks across the pad, and that walk is one of the earliest signals you get, well before the part is visibly moving.

The obvious implementation does not work and it is worth knowing why. Differencing consecutive frames on this pad, with 60 micrometres of cell jitter and a 10 ms frame, reports about 9 mm per second of drift on a contact that is not moving at all. The slip you are trying to catch is 4 mm per second. The noise is louder than the signal by a factor of two, and no threshold separates them.

So difference across a **window** instead. With `WINDOW` frames between the two samples the jitter is unchanged but the time is twenty times longer, so the noise floor falls by twenty while the real drift does not move: `drift = float(np.linalg.norm(frames[k] - frames[k - WINDOW]))` and the test is `drift / (WINDOW * DT) > DRIFT_LIMIT`. The price is latency, 200 ms of it here, which is why the buzz detector of two lessons from now exists.

The demonstration runs both recordings through the windowed detector and prints the per frame figure next to it. Read the false alarm count on the firm hold, because that is the number that decides whether anybody leaves your detector switched on.

import numpy as np

DT = 0.010
WINDOW = 20
DRIFT_LIMIT = 0.0025
FRAMES = 200
JITTER = 0.000060
SLIDE_SPEED = 0.004


def recording(sliding, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = []
    for k in range(FRAMES):
        base = np.array([0.0, -SLIDE_SPEED * k * DT if sliding else 0.0])
        out.append(base + rng.normal(0.0, JITTER, 2))
    return out


def per_frame_speed(frames, k):
    return float(np.linalg.norm(frames[k] - frames[k - 1])) / DT


def drift_speed(frames, k):
    drift = float(np.linalg.norm(frames[k] - frames[k - WINDOW]))
    return drift / (WINDOW * DT)


def is_slipping(frames, k):
    drift = float(np.linalg.norm(frames[k] - frames[k - WINDOW]))
    return bool(drift / (WINDOW * DT) > DRIFT_LIMIT)

    frames = recording(sliding, seed)

lessons.title: Sliding Before It Slides
lessons.goal: Compute how much of the friction cone a contact is using and raise a warning before the whole contact lets go.
lessons.theory:
A contact does not go from stuck to sliding in one step. The edge of the patch starts sliding first while the middle is still stuck, and that state, **incipient slip**, is the last moment at which squeezing harder still fixes anything.

The number that tracks it is how much of the cone the contact is spending: `ratio = ft / (mu * fn)`, zero when the contact is pushing straight in and one at the instant of gross slip. The reason to act at 0.7 rather than at 1.0 is that everything upstream is late. The tactile frame is 10 ms old, the controller runs at 50 Hz, and the gripper takes 80 ms to change its force meaningfully. By the time a ratio of 1.0 has been read, acted on and executed, the part has moved.

lessons.title: The Buzz of Sliding
lessons.goal: Detect slip from the high frequency energy of a tactile signal instead of from its mean level.
lessons.theory:
Rubber sliding on a rigid part does not slide smoothly. It sticks, releases, sticks again, hundreds of times a second, and that stick slip cycle puts a buzz into the tactile signal that a mean pressure reading averages straight out.

You do not need a spectrum to find it. Take the first difference of the window, `diffs = np.diff(window)`, which throws away everything slow and keeps everything fast, and measure its size with `float(np.sqrt(np.mean(diffs ** 2)))`. That number is small on a firm hold, where the only fast content is cell noise, and several times larger while sliding.

The detector this gives you is faster than watching the centre of pressure move, because the buzz starts with the first stick slip cycle and the drift needs several frames to accumulate. It also needs a fast sensor: sampling at 100 Hz throws the whole signal away, so this is a 1 kHz measurement or it is nothing.

The demonstration takes one recording with a firm segment and a sliding segment at the same mean pressure. Compare the means, which say nothing, against the difference energies, which are what you would trigger on.

lessons.goal: Estimate the real friction coefficient from a recorded slip event and recompute the squeeze the part actually needs.
lessons.theory:
Every slip is a free measurement, and it is the only honest one you will get. At the instant the part let go, the contact was exactly on the edge of its cone, so the ratio of the two forces at that instant **is** the friction coefficient: `estimate = ft_at_slip / fn_at_slip`.

lessons.title: Squeeze Only When It Slips
lessons.goal: Build an adaptive grip controller that steps the force up on a slip event and lets it decay back down between events.
lessons.theory:
Holding everything at maximum force is a policy, and it is the one most cells run. It marks soft parts, wears pads, costs cycle time on release, and it is what you do when you have no slip sensing. With slip sensing you can do the thing a human hand does instead, which is to hold as lightly as possible and firm up the moment something moves.

The controller is two lines and no tuning subtlety. On a slip event, jump: `force = min(FORCE_MAX, force + SLIP_STEP)`. Every other cycle, bleed off: `force = max(FORCE_MIN, force - DECAY * DT)`. The step has to be large enough to actually stop the slip in one go, because a controller that creeps up while the part is moving loses the part, and the decay has to be slow enough that it does not undo the last correction before the next disturbance.

What comes out is a staircase that finds the right force by itself and follows the real friction coefficient as it changes during the move. It also gives you a diagnostic for free: the number of slip events in a cycle is a health signal, and a part that used to need one correction and now needs four is telling you the pads are finished.

The demonstration transports a part through two disturbances and prints the force history. Compare the peak force it reaches against the fixed maximum a non adaptive gripper would have used for the whole move.

lessons.title: It Turned in the Hand
lessons.goal: Distinguish an object translating through the fingers from one rotating between them, using two tactile pads.
lessons.theory:
One pad cannot tell you whether the part slid or turned. Two can, and the test is a sign.

When the part slides through the jaws, both centres of pressure walk the **same** way, because both pads are being dragged over the same moving surface. When the part turns about an axis between the fingers, they walk **opposite** ways, one up and one down. So the rotation estimate is the difference of the two, scaled by the distance between the pads: `rotation = (cop_a - cop_b) / (2.0 * HALF_SPAN)` radians, and the translation estimate is their average.

The reason to separate them is that the corrections are different. A translation is answered with more squeeze. A rotation is answered with more squeeze **and** usually a regrasp, because a part that has turned in the jaws is no longer where the placement routine believes it is, and squeezing harder freezes the error in place.

lessons.title: The Pose You Think It Is
lessons.goal: Compute where the pads actually land when the estimated part pose is wrong, and decide whether the grasp still lands on the part.
lessons.theory:
Every grasp so far assumed the part was exactly where the estimate said. It is not. A calibrated camera at 600 mm gives you a couple of millimetres on a good day, a part sitting on a chamfer adds a couple more, and nothing in the pipeline tells you which day it is.

The geometry is simple and the consequence is not. If the jaws close at the estimated centre and the part is somewhere else, the pads land at `offset = estimated[1] - actual[1]` from the part centre, along the part. The grasp is still on the part while `abs(offset) <= 0.5 * PART_LENGTH - PAD_HALF`, and the moment arm the grip has to fight grows by exactly that offset, which is the calculation from the third chapter arriving with real numbers.

So a pose error does two things at once. It walks the contacts towards the end of the part, and it puts the grip off the centre of mass. The first one has a hard edge where the pads fall off the part entirely. The second degrades smoothly and is the one that produces intermittent failures nobody can reproduce.

The demonstration walks the error out on a 60 mm bar with 16 mm pads and prints both consequences at each step.

lessons.title: The Jaws Put It Back
lessons.goal: Decide whether a closing chamfered jaw can slide a misplaced part into the centre against table friction.
lessons.theory:
Closing jaws are not only a clamp, they are a funnel. A chamfered or V shaped jaw face turns the closing motion into a sideways push on the part, and if that push beats the friction holding the part to the table, the part slides into the middle by itself. That is why a well designed finger recovers pose error for free and a flat finger does not.

The lateral push a chamfer produces from a given closing force is `push = force * math.tan(math.radians(CHAMFER_DEG))`. A 30 degree chamfer converts 58 percent of the squeeze into sideways travel. A 10 degree one converts 18 percent, and a flat face converts nothing, which is the whole design argument in one line.

What it has to beat is the part sitting on the table: `push > MU_TABLE * mass * G`. Note what is missing from that inequality. The part mass matters, the table finish matters, and the pose error does not, so the funnel either works for this part or it never works, and testing it once tells you.

The demonstration runs three closing forces on a 600 g part on a steel table with a 30 degree chamfer. The lightest one does not move the part at all, which on the cell floor looks like the gripper closing normally and the part ending up crooked.

lessons.title: Pushing Turns It
lessons.goal: Predict which way a pushed part rotates from the moment of the push about its centre of friction.
lessons.theory:
Sometimes the right move is not to grasp at all. Pushing a part across a table is how you separate it from a neighbour, bring it out from a wall, or turn it into an orientation you can pick. To do that on purpose you have to predict which way it turns.

For a part sliding on a table the useful reference is the **centre of friction**, which for a part of uniform density on a uniform table is its centre of mass. The push produces a moment about that point, and in the plane that moment is the one scalar `moment = r[0] * f[1] - r[1] * f[0]`, where `r` is from the centre of friction to the push point. Its sign is the answer, and `int(np.sign(moment))` is the whole prediction: positive turns anticlockwise, negative clockwise, zero means the part translates without turning.

The zero case is the useful one. A push whose line of action passes through the centre of friction moves the part in a straight line, and hitting that line on purpose is how a pushing routine positions a part without scrambling its orientation. Miss it by a few millimetres and the part arrives rotated, which is why pushing is usually followed by another look from the camera.

lessons.title: How Fast You Are Allowed to Move
lessons.goal: Compute the largest transport acceleration a grip survives, from the squeeze and the friction coefficient.
lessons.theory:
A grip that holds a part standing still is not a grip that holds it through a move. During transport the part needs a force of `mass` times the vector sum of gravity and the acceleration, and the fingers have `2 * mu * fn` of friction to supply all of it.

lessons.title: Squeeze Harder or Move Slower

The last lesson answered how fast you may move at a given squeeze. Turn it round and you get the question a cell scheduler asks, which is how hard to squeeze for the move it already wants to make.

lessons.title: Regrasp or Carry On
lessons.goal: Turn slip margin, pose drift and in hand rotation into one ordered recovery decision.
lessons.theory:
By now you can measure four things about a grip in flight: how much of the friction cone it is using, how far the contact has drifted, how far the part has turned in the jaws, and whether the mass is what it should be. A cell needs one decision out of them, and the decision has more than two values.

The order defends itself. `if not mass_ok:` comes first and returns `"abort"`, because if the wrong thing is in the hand nothing else matters and continuing puts an unknown part into an assembly. Then the cone ratio, which is a grip that is merely too light and is answered by `"squeeze"` without stopping the move. Everything else carries on.

What that ordering buys is that the expensive recoveries are only reached when the cheap ones cannot help. Reverse the last two and every rotation gets answered with more force, the part stays crooked, and the placement fails downstream where it is much harder to diagnose.
