lessons.goal: Release a part only once the surface has taken its weight, and measure what releasing too early costs.
lessons.theory:
A place is a pick run backwards and it has one extra failure mode that a pick does not: the moment of release. Open the jaws while the arm is still pressing and the stored energy in the arm, the pad and the part goes somewhere, and where it goes is the part.

The signal is the wrist. As the part lands, the surface takes its weight, so what the arm is carrying falls from the part weight towards zero and then goes negative as the arm starts pressing: `wrist = PART_WEIGHT - K_TABLE * max(0.0, CONTACT_Z - z)`. The right moment to open is when the surface has the load and the arm is neither lifting nor pressing, which is `abs(wrist) <= UNLOAD_BAND`.

The policy this replaces is the common one: descend a fixed distance below the nominal surface and open there. Even with a **perfect** surface estimate, the 2 mm of commanded depth that policy uses is 94 N of press on a 50000 newton per metre bench at the instant the fingers let go, and every millimetre of estimate error adds 50 N to that.

The demonstration runs both policies down the same descent, with a surface estimate that is exactly right, so the whole difference is the policy. lessons.title: What the Gripper Can Even Reach
lessons.goal: Filter the bin on stroke, payload and wall clearance, and return a specific reason for each refusal.
lessons.theory:
The first filter is the hardware one and it has nothing to do with grasp quality. Either the gripper physically fits around the part and can carry it, or the rest of the pipeline is wasted work.

Four tests, and each one gets its own message, because a refusal that says `"no"` sends an engineer to read code and a refusal that names the number sends them to the right drawing. The stroke test is `width + 2.0 * (PAD_THICKNESS + APPROACH_GAP) <= MAX_OPENING` from the fifth chapter with the pads counted, and its twin at the other end of the range is the jaw floor. The payload test is the rating from the very first lesson of the course. The wall test is the clearance from the eighth: a part with less than a jaw of room needs a push before it needs a grasp, so the refusal is `return "needs a push off the wall"` and it is an instruction rather than a dead end.

Order them so the cheapest and most final comes first. Stroke, then the floor, then payload, then the wall, because the first three are properties of the part that will not change and the last is a property of this cycle that a push can fix.

The second filter belongs to the part rather than to the gripper, and it is the one that catches the foam.

        force = STIFFNESS * max(0.0, surface_z - z)
        peak = max(peak, force)
        if force >= FORCE_THRESHOLD:
            return z, peak
    return None, peak


def verdict(width, force, taxels):
    if width <= EMPTY_WIDTH:
        return "empty"
    if force < MIN_FORCE:
        return "not loaded"
    if taxels < MIN_TAXELS:
        return "edge contact"
    return "held"


for name, surface_z, width, force, taxels in CASES:
    contact_z, peak = descend(surface_z)
    print(name, "contact at mm", "none found" if contact_z is None else round(contact_z * 1000.0, 2),
          "peak N", round(peak, 2), "close verdict", verdict(width, force, taxels))
lessons.hint: In `descend` the guard replaces the `pass` and returns `z, peak`. In `verdict` the three guards go above the `return "held"`: `if width <= EMPTY_WIDTH:` returns `"empty"`, `if force < MIN_FORCE:` returns `"not loaded"`, and `if taxels < MIN_TAXELS:` returns `"edge contact"`.

lessons.title: Carrying It Without Losing It
lessons.goal: Cap the transport acceleration to what the grip supports and step the squeeze up when the slip monitor fires.
lessons.theory:
The part is in the hand and the move is the part of the cycle where it gets dropped. Two mechanisms from the last two chapters do the work, and they answer different failures.

The first is planning. `a_max = math.sqrt(max(0.0, (2.0 * mu * squeeze / mass) ** 2 - G ** 2))` is the largest acceleration the current squeeze survives, and the move is capped at it rather than at what the arm can do. That is a decision made before the arm moves and it costs cycle time honestly.

The second is reaction. Nothing above knows the real friction coefficient, so a slip monitor watches anyway and `force = min(FORCE_MAX, force + SLIP_STEP)` firms the grip when it fires. Between events the squeeze decays back down, so a part that never slips is never crushed.

The demonstration carries the three survivors at a planned 2.0 g. One of them cannot have it, because its squeeze was clamped by the crush limit rather than chosen for the move, and it is carried slower. Another slips once on the way and is caught. The report says which is which. A cell that logs those two facts per cycle can be tuned by somebody who was not there.

lessons.title: The Order Goes Out
lessons.goal: Run the whole bin through every stage and report the parts placed, the parts refused and the reason for each refusal.
lessons.theory:
Everything joins here. Seven parts go in, four stages run, and what comes out is a placed count, a refusal list with a reason on every line, and the sentence a shift supervisor can act on.

The structure is the one that survives contact with a real cell. Each stage is a function that returns either `None` or a reason, the loop stops at the first reason, and both outcomes are recorded: `refusals.append((name, reason))` for the ones that stop and `placed = placed + 1` for the ones that finish. Nothing is silently skipped, which is the property that makes the report worth reading at all.

Read the refusal list as three different jobs for three different people. A part wider than the stroke is a tooling order. A part with no force window is a pad order. A part against the wall is a motion the cell can perform today and simply has not been programmed to, and it is the one worth doing next.

This is the end of the workshop. What you have is a pick pipeline that refuses for stated reasons, sizes its own grip, stops on contact instead of on faith, and reacts to slip. Every number in it came from a lesson, and none of it needed a gripper that costs more than the arm.
